corpus_purpose: A prompt-time reasoning and language corpus for OpenAI generation. It teaches Adoption, Workforce, and Economic Outcomes as separate platform domains built from one integrated acquisition effort spanning microeconomic use, organizational production, labor transmission, firm outcomes, and macroeconomic aggregation. It does not provide runtime facts and must not deterministically rewrite generated prose.

runtime_boundary.academic_sources: Analytical and rhetorical guidance only; never substitute paper quantities for current platform evidence.
runtime_boundary.long_form_sources: Production-form and boundary guidance only; manuscript quantities are not injected as current facts unless independently present in the runtime evidence packet.
runtime_boundary.generation_contract: All corpus rules and current evidence are supplied to OpenAI before generation. Domain Reads are generated first; the paid domain outputs and evidence then feed the paid AI Macro roll-up. No hidden replacement call, automatic retry, fallback generation, or post-generation prose mutation is authorized.
runtime_boundary.domain_separation: Adoption, Workforce, and Economic Outcomes share a reasoning architecture but retain separate titles, evidence packets, instructions, and outputs.

journal_gate.rule: Admit peer-reviewed journal articles that satisfy the project's journal-quality gate and complete-substantive-text requirement.

counting_rules.source: One final peer-reviewed article with one verified identity counts once, even when multiple versions were reviewed.
counting_rules.observation: One indivisible, source-bounded analytical proposition with a traceable source and family assignment counts once.
counting_rules.family: One reusable reasoning rule that cannot be reduced to an existing family counts once.

methodology.full_text_rule: Admission required complete substantive access and review of framing, methods, results, discussion, limitations, appendices, and genre-equivalent sections.
methodology.saturation_rule: Two consecutive independent five-paper challenge batches must add no more than two universal families each and reopen no foundation gap; a five-paper integrated confirmation must fit the resulting framework without expansion.
methodology.long_form_rule: Two complete long-form texts and approximately fourteen passage analyses; store learned analytical moves rather than copied passages.
methodology.rights_boundary: Store structured observations, provenance, and learned form rather than copyrighted prose.

verified_admissions.title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 53-page Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis author manuscript reconciled to the published INFORMS record

verified_extraction.claim_path: representative person-level use -> frequency and work-hours intensity -> reported task assistance and time savings
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Two nationally representative 2024 U.S. surveys totaling more than 10,000 respondents age 18-64; employed-worker denominators are separated from all-adult denominators
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Use and implied productivity potential vary by occupation, industry, education, age, and firm climate
limitations: Self-reported use and time savings are not instrumented production outcomes
Late-2024 conditions do not describe later model capabilities or current platform data
Worker-reported use is not equivalent to employer deployment

verified_admissions.title: AI adoption in America: Who, what, and where

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Census/NBER institutional manuscript reconciled to Wiley publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: production-use definition -> establishment/firm adoption -> size-weighted diffusion -> concentration among large firms
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 2018 Annual Business Survey sent to roughly 850,000 U.S. firms and linked to Census longitudinal business data; firm-weighted and employment-weighted rates are distinct
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Adoption is much higher among very large firms and varies with firm age, owner education and experience, industry, and geography
limitations: Measures five pre-generative-AI technologies around 2017-2018
Cross-sectional adoption patterns do not establish productivity effects
A firm-weighted rate cannot be compared directly with an employment-weighted rate

verified_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence adoption and system-wide change

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Wiley article text and complete author record

verified_extraction.claim_path: task-level prediction improvement -> increased decision variation -> interaction with organizational interdependence -> coordination or modular redesign
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Formal multi-decision organizational model, not an empirical adoption estimate
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Interdependencies can impede adoption without coordination yet raise adoption value when coordination mechanisms exist
limitations: Theoretical propositions are not observed firm outcomes
The result depends on modeled interdependence and coordination costs
Task-level capability cannot be treated as system-level implementation

verified_admissions.title: Experimental evidence on the productivity effects of generative artificial intelligence

whole_text_audit.access: Complete MIT author manuscript reconciled to Science publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: random access to ChatGPT -> task completion time and blind quality scores -> within-task productivity and distribution
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 453 college-educated professionals completing incentivized mid-level professional writing tasks
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Lower initial performers gain more, compressing the measured productivity distribution
limitations: Short, bounded writing tasks are not jobs or complete workflows
Participants and tasks do not represent the whole workforce
Time and quality gains do not directly establish firm revenue, profit, wages, or employment

verified_admissions.title: Generative AI at Work

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Oxford Academic article HTML and replication record

verified_extraction.claim_path: production deployment -> suggestion access and adherence -> speed, resolution, quality, learning, and work-experience outcomes
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Staggered rollout to 5,172 customer-support agents at one Fortune 500 software firm and its contractors
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Large gains accrue to novice and lower-skill agents; top agents see little speed gain and a small quality decline
limitations: One firm, one occupation, and one tool
Medium-run partial-equilibrium evidence does not identify wages or aggregate labor demand
Attrition estimates lack worker fixed effects and warrant more caution

verified_admissions.title: AI, Skill, and Productivity: The Case of Taxi Drivers

whole_text_audit.access: Complete INFORMS article HTML

verified_extraction.claim_path: voluntary predictive-AI use -> customer-search time -> driver productivity by prior skill
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 520 Yokohama taxi drivers offered a 29-day free trial; search time is the primary outcome
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Average search-time improvement is concentrated among lower-skill drivers, with near-zero effect for higher-skill drivers
limitations: Short trial in one city and occupation
Voluntary take-up creates selection addressed but not eliminated by design and IV checks
Search-time gains need not translate one-for-one into daily income or labor demand

verified_admissions.title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access article through PubMed Central and Science Advances

verified_extraction.claim_path: access to one or five AI-generated ideas -> individual story ratings -> cross-story similarity
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 293 writers and 600 blinded evaluators in a short-story experiment
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Writers with lower baseline creativity receive the largest individual gains; highly creative writers are not supercharged
limitations: Short stories are not firm innovation or commercial products
Uniform AI inputs and task design may contribute to homogenization
Higher ratings do not establish downstream market value

verified_admissions.title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers

whole_text_audit.access: Complete MIT/Microsoft author manuscript reconciled to INFORMS publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: random coding-assistant access -> actual take-up -> completed development tasks
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Three workplace randomized trials totaling 4,867 developers at Microsoft, Accenture, and a Fortune 100 firm
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Less-experienced developers adopt more and obtain larger estimated gains; separate experiments are noisy
limitations: Pooled estimate masks cross-company imprecision and heterogeneity
Completed tasks do not fully measure code quality, maintainability, or business value
Access is not identical to sustained workflow integration

verified_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence, firm growth, and product innovation

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 89-page author manuscript reconciled to the open-access JFE record and replication package

verified_extraction.claim_path: AI-skilled labor investment proxy -> later sales, employment, valuation, and innovation -> firm and industry distribution
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. public and private firms observed through worker resumes, job postings, financial records, and innovation measures over 2010-2018
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Growth and product-innovation gains concentrate among ex-ante larger firms, increasing concentration
limitations: AI-skilled hiring is an investment proxy, not direct observation of deployed use
The instrument and no-pretrend tests support but do not make every estimate experimental
Firm growth can include business stealing and does not imply aggregate net growth

verified_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence and firm-level productivity

whole_text_audit.access: Complete KU Leuven institutional manuscript reconciled to Elsevier publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: surveyed AI use and intensity -> firm production-function estimates -> productivity association
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: German firm survey and panel data with multiple AI-use measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Results are tested across adoption indicator and intensity measures and under cross-sectional, panel, and IV specifications
limitations: Country and survey context constrain external validity
Positive significant estimates do not measure worker incidence or aggregate spillovers
Instrument validity and self-reported adoption remain material identification considerations

verified_admissions.title: Occupational, industry, and geographic exposure to artificial intelligence: A novel dataset and its potential uses

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Wiley article text and Princeton repository record

verified_extraction.claim_path: AI application progress -> occupational abilities -> occupation exposure -> industry and geography aggregation
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Ten AI applications mapped to 52 O*NET abilities and then to occupation employment structures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Exposure can be aggregated differently by occupation, industry, county, and firm workforce composition
limitations: Exposure is direction-neutral and cannot distinguish complementarity from substitution
The measure does not observe adoption, task change, wages, employment, or displacement
Aggregation inherits O*NET and employment-weighting assumptions

verified_admissions.title: GPTs are GPTs: Labor market impact potential of LLMs

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Science PDF and author manuscript

verified_extraction.claim_path: task descriptions -> modeled time-saving capability under quality constraint -> occupation-level potential exposure
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. O*NET tasks evaluated under human and model rubrics for direct LLM and LLM-powered-software scenarios
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Potential exposure spans wage levels and is higher in many higher-income knowledge occupations
limitations: The paper explicitly does not predict adoption timing
Potential exposure is not observed use, automation, displacement, or employment loss
Results depend on task descriptions, capability thresholds, and modeled software complementarity

verified_admissions.title: New Frontiers: The Origins and Content of New Work, 1940-2018

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 67-page Oxford Academic PDF

verified_extraction.claim_path: augmentation or automation innovation -> new work creation -> occupational employment and wagebill
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Eight decades of U.S. job titles linked to Census microdata and patent-text measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: New-work creation shifts from middle-paid production and clerical work before 1980 toward high-paid professional and lower-paid services after 1980
limitations: Historical technology evidence is not a direct estimate of generative AI
Patent-text exposure measures innovation direction, not current deployment
Long-run occupation responses cannot be mapped mechanically onto short-run platform indicators

verified_admissions.title: Artificial intelligence and jobs: evidence from US commuting zones

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 50-page Oxford Academic PDF

verified_extraction.claim_path: local industry composition and national AI adoption -> commuting-zone AI exposure -> employment-rate changes
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. commuting zones over 2000-2020 using a shift-share design
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Estimated employment effects are more negative in services, for lower-skill and production workers, and positive at the top of the wage distribution
limitations: Period largely predates mass-market generative AI
Shift-share estimates rely on exclusion and composition assumptions
Local relative effects need not equal national aggregate employment effects

verified_admissions.title: The simple macroeconomics of AI

whole_text_audit.access: Complete Economic Policy issue PDF

verified_extraction.claim_path: share of tasks affected x task-level cost savings -> calibrated aggregate TFP and GDP path -> wage and inequality incidence
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Model-based calibration using published task-exposure and micro-productivity evidence over a ten-year horizon
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Hard-to-learn, context-dependent tasks reduce plausible aggregate gains relative to easy benchmark tasks; wage effects differ by demographic and occupational exposure
limitations: Calibration is a scenario, not an observed forecast track
Inputs inherit uncertainty from exposure measures and selected micro studies
Task cost savings are not automatically realized without adoption and complementary change

verified_admissions.title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of Artificial Intelligence on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality

whole_text_audit.access: Complete INFORMS article HTML and online-appendix record

verified_extraction.claim_path: random GPT-4 access with or without an overview -> behavior on realistic consulting tasks -> completion, speed, quality, and correctness on opposite sides of a task frontier
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 758 BCG consultants split across two nonoverlapping experimental arms; the inside-frontier arm contains eighteen subtasks and the outside-frontier arm contains one objectively scored strategic recommendation
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: AI raised completion, speed, and quality inside the tested frontier but reduced correctness outside it; effects depend on task position, workflow behavior, evaluation metric, and incentive setting
limitations: One elite professional-services workforce
Only one deliberately selected outside-frontier task
Subjective rubrics are necessary for several inside-frontier outputs
A laboratory-in-the-field task bundle is not a full production deployment
The tested GPT-4 capability frontier can move over time

anti_patterns: Do not report an average AI productivity effect without identifying the task side of the capability frontier.
Do not infer reliable judgment from gains in ideation, writing, or analysis.
Do not treat a prompt overview as proof that training eliminates automation bias.

verified_admissions.title: The Short-Term Effects of Generative Artificial Intelligence on Employment: Evidence from an Online Labor Market

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 24-page CESifo institutional manuscript reconciled to the Organization Science publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: public generative-AI release -> relative change for freelancers in more- versus less-affected occupations -> platform jobs, employment probability, conditional jobs, and earnings
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 92,547 searchable single-occupation Upwork freelancers observed monthly from January 2022 through April 2023, with a separate image-occupation analysis around image-model releases
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Short-run adverse platform outcomes extend across measured prior-quality groups and may be larger for top workers; writing and image markets provide separate shocks
limitations: The design observes platform work rather than total employment or off-platform income
The sample is a flexible spot market, not conventional payroll employment
Profiles are observed as an April 2023 snapshot and terminated or nonsearchable accounts are missing
Occupation treatment depends on exposure classification and common-trend assumptions
Short-run substitution need not predict longer-run complementarity, entry, demand, or equilibrium adjustment

anti_patterns: Do not relabel fewer platform contracts as economy-wide job loss.
Do not relabel platform earnings as hourly wages.
Do not assume prior quality insulates workers from a technology shock.
Do not extrapolate a short post-release window into a permanent labor-market effect.

verified_admissions.title: Skill Deprioritization: Reorganizing in the Age of Generative Artificial Intelligence

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access INFORMS article HTML and supplemental-material record

verified_extraction.claim_path: firm occupational exposure and public GenAI availability -> changes in postings for organizing skills -> selective early skill deprioritization
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Job-posting demand at 1,820 publicly listed U.S. companies in a plus-or-minus twelve-month window around ChatGPT, with comparisons between more- and less-exposed firms
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Demand falls for task division, information provision, monitoring, and operational exceptions, while task allocation, incentive design, and conflict resolution remain statistically more stable; effects intensify after GPT-4
limitations: Job postings measure desired hiring demand rather than filled jobs, incumbent tasks, or realized reorganization
ChatGPT is treated as an availability shock and exposure is assigned from occupation composition
The short window captures early response rather than long-run organizational equilibrium
Public firms may not represent small or private employers
Capability improvements and contemporaneous labor-demand changes may be difficult to isolate fully

anti_patterns: Do not call a decline in a skill-tagged posting an observed elimination of that skill inside firms.
Do not collapse all managerial functions into one automation category.
Do not turn statistically stable categories into proof of permanent human exclusivity.

verified_admissions.title: Curse or Blessing: Investigating the Influence of Firms' Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Employee Job Satisfaction

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access Wiley article and author-repository record

verified_extraction.claim_path: firm-level AI-adoption intensity -> changing balance of job enrichment and impairment -> employee job satisfaction, conditional on exploration orientation and data governance
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: 509 publicly listed U.S. firms from 2009 through 2020 linked to more than 2.4 million Glassdoor reviews, supplemented by eleven follow-up employee interviews
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Estimated job satisfaction rises at moderate adoption and declines at high adoption; exploration orientation moves the turning point and data governance dampens the curvature
limitations: AI adoption is proxied from earnings-call discussion rather than direct system-use telemetry
Glassdoor reviewers are self-selected and firm-level aggregation masks occupation and worker differences
The panel predates mass-market generative AI
The inverted-U estimate is observational and sensitive to functional form and measurement
Eleven interviews illuminate mechanisms but are not population estimates

anti_patterns: Do not assume more AI adoption monotonically improves employee welfare.
Do not equate job satisfaction with productivity, pay, autonomy, or retention.
Do not treat governance as a generic positive control without specifying what it moderates.

verified_admissions.title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption and the Demand for Managerial Expertise

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 27-page open-access Wiley article

verified_extraction.claim_path: firm AI-skill hiring intensity -> managerial vacancy quantity and share -> changes in demanded managerial skills
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: U.S. firm job postings from 2010 through 2022 drawn from a universe of nearly 375 million vacancies; AI adoption is proxied by the share of vacancies requesting AI skills
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Managerial demand rises most in manufacturing and R&D-intensive firms, while skill demand shifts from routine administration toward stakeholder management, creativity, sales management, and data analysis
limitations: AI-skill vacancies proxy investment or adoption rather than installed systems or use intensity
Vacancies are labor demand, not hiring, employment, task execution, or wages
Firm matching and minimum-posting thresholds alter the estimation sample
Instrumental-variable estimates depend on exclusion and relevance assumptions
Associations through 2022 only begin to cover the generative-AI regime

anti_patterns: Do not infer managerial displacement from automation of selected administrative skills.
Do not infer filled employment from posted vacancies.
Do not treat an AI-skill share as direct observation of deployment depth.

verified_admissions.title: New Technologies and Jobs in Europe

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 59-page Banco de España institutional manuscript and November 2024 author draft reconciled to the Economic Policy publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: occupation-level potential exposure to AI and software -> changes in sector-occupation employment shares and relative wages -> variation by worker composition and national institutions
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Three-digit occupations in sector-occupation cells across fifteen euro-area countries and the United Kingdom from 2011 through 2019, using EU-LFS employment and wage measures
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Employment shares rise on average in more AI-exposed occupations, especially those with younger and more-skilled workers; wage evidence is weak, and national results vary with diffusion, education, product-market regulation, and employment protection
limitations: Exposure indices do not observe firm adoption or generative-AI use
The estimates are associations at occupation-sector level rather than randomized causal effects
Employment-share changes need not equal changes in employment levels
The 2011-2019 period predates mass-market generative AI
Cross-country correlates are suggestive and may reflect omitted institutional differences

anti_patterns: Do not treat potential exposure as observed adoption.
Do not relabel an employment-share change as net job creation.
Do not infer wage gains from employment-share gains.
Do not erase country, skill, or age heterogeneity behind the pooled coefficient.

verified_admissions.title: Concentrating Intelligence: Scaling and Market Structure in Artificial Intelligence

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 32-page INET author manuscript reconciled to the Economic Policy publication

verified_extraction.claim_path: high fixed training and adaptation costs plus low operating costs, scarce inputs, and scope economies -> provider competition, entry barriers, tipping, and vertical integration -> market power and distribution of AI value
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Industrial-organization analysis of the foundation-model stack using market, cost, input, investment, and capability evidence available through September 2024
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Fierce model-level competition can coexist with concentrated compute and cloud inputs; open-source distribution, capability convergence, breakthroughs, demand scale, and vertical ties can change contestability
limitations: The market snapshot ages quickly in a rapidly changing industry
Several cost, share, and investment observations rely on external estimates rather than audited public accounts
Natural-monopoly tendencies are mechanisms and scenarios, not proof of a durable monopoly
Transformative-AI implications are explicitly speculative
Policy effects are analyzed rather than empirically identified

anti_patterns: Do not equate high fixed costs with observed monopoly.
Do not infer broad welfare from provider revenue or valuation.
Do not treat current market share as durable when capabilities, prices, and open-source alternatives are moving.
Do not ignore upstream compute and cloud concentration when describing model competition.

verified_admissions.title: When Does AI Pay Off? AI-Adoption Intensity, Complementary Investments, and R&D Strategy

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 15-page published article PDF and author manuscript

verified_extraction.claim_path: surveyed NLP, computer-vision, or machine-learning adoption intensity -> firm revenue growth -> moderation by database, cloud, and firm-specific R&D investment
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: High-tech ventures in South Korea surveyed in 2019 and linked to administrative and retrospectively reported firm characteristics; the main growth sample is a selected subset of surviving firms
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Low adoption intensity is not significantly related to revenue growth; positive associations appear at higher intensity and chiefly among ventures with complementary data, cloud, and internal R&D capabilities
limitations: The observational design cannot eliminate omitted-variable or reverse-causality bias
Adoption intensity is self-reported in broad categories
The analysis assumes little or no AI adoption at the retrospective base year
Revenue growth is not productivity, profit, wages, or welfare
High-tech South Korean ventures are not representative of all firms or countries

anti_patterns: Do not treat testing or low-intensity use as evidence of realized firm payoff.
Do not infer causality from the revenue-growth association.
Do not generalize a high-tech venture threshold mechanically to large incumbents or other countries.
Do not omit the complementary data, cloud, and R&D conditions.

verified_admissions.title: The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 55-page NBER author manuscript reconciled to the AEA publication and replication record

verified_extraction.claim_path: new general-purpose technology -> complementary intangible investment and foregone current output -> later capital services -> difference between true and measured productivity across the adoption cycle
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Formal growth-accounting model applied to U.S. computer-hardware and software capital using national accounts and estimated intangible complements through 2017
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Measured productivity can understate true productivity during intangible-capital formation and overstate it when previously accumulated complements yield services; timing and magnitude depend on investment and depreciation assumptions
limitations: Empirical calibration uses earlier computer hardware and software rather than realized generative-AI investment
Many organization, training, data, and process intangibles are unobserved and modeled
The J-curve is a measurement mechanism, not a guarantee of eventual payoff
National-account treatment differs from firm accounting and from welfare measurement
Results depend on capital-service, depreciation, and counterfactual assumptions

anti_patterns: Do not use the J-curve to excuse every weak productivity result.
Do not call all current spending productive intangible capital.
Do not infer future gains unless complementary assets are actually accumulated and produce services.
Do not confuse measured TFP, true productivity, output, and welfare.

verified_admissions.title: Artificial Intelligence and Jobs: Evidence from Online Vacancies

whole_text_audit.access: Complete 49-page MIT open-access final published version

verified_extraction.claim_path: establishment task suitability -> posting of AI vacancies as an adoption proxy -> changes in non-AI hiring and requested skills -> tests for aggregate occupation and industry employment and wages
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Near-universe of U.S. online vacancies from 2010 through 2018 linked at establishment, firm, occupation, industry, commuting-zone, and skill levels
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: AI-adopting exposed establishments reduce non-AI vacancy posting and alter requested skills, yet aggregate employment and wage effects in exposed occupations and industries remain too small to detect in the sample period
limitations: Vacancies measure intended hiring rather than filled jobs, incumbent employment, or task execution
AI vacancies are a narrow adoption proxy and miss systems deployed without AI hiring
The study predates mass-market generative AI
Establishment effects can be offset by reallocation, entry, demand, and spillovers elsewhere
Statistically undetectable aggregate effects are not proof of zero effect

anti_patterns: Do not promote an establishment hiring response into an aggregate employment claim.
Do not treat absence of a detectable aggregate coefficient as proof of no effect.
Do not equate AI vacancies with installed AI or use intensity.
Do not equate requested skills, vacancies, hires, employment, and wages.

verified_admissions.title: The Cybernetic Teammate: A Field Experiment on Generative AI and Teamwork

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access INFORMS article, pages 1217-1242, including supplemental record
sections_reviewed: discussion, caveats, scope conditions, and conclusion

verified_extraction.claim_path: random assignment of consumer-goods professionals to individual or cross-functional team work with or without a fixed GenAI tool -> generated product-development solution quality, expertise balance, idea selection, and self-reported experience -> implications for selected collaborative functions and work design
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: One-day virtual product-development workshop at Procter & Gamble; 776 of 791 completers supplied full post-task data, while the principal quality regressions use 550 randomized solution records because team members share one submitted solution
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Individuals with AI reached average quality comparable to non-AI pairs and crossed functional boundaries more readily; teams with AI did not significantly exceed individuals with AI on average but were more likely to produce top-decile solutions; AI improved idea quality more clearly than selection accuracy
limitations: The experiment covers one company, one industry, one early-stage innovation task, and one AI model at one date
One-day remote flash teams do not reproduce persistent teams, embedded relationships, iterative rework, or face-to-face interaction
Participants were relatively inexperienced prompt users and the tool was not purpose-built for collaboration
The design cannot cleanly decompose augmentation of noncollaborative work from substitution for collaborative functions
Solution ratings and top-decile probability do not establish launch, revenue, profit, employment, or economy-wide productivity

anti_patterns: Do not claim that one AI user universally replaces a team.
Do not translate higher rated concepts into commercialized products or firm performance.
Do not erase the weaker idea-selection result behind the higher average-quality result.
Do not generalize a one-day single-firm experiment to sustained organizational redesign.

verified_admissions.title: Roles of Artificial Intelligence in Collaboration with Humans: Automation, Augmentation, and the Future of Work

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access INFORMS article, pages 538-557, including online appendix and data references

verified_extraction.claim_path: relative human and AI performance plus between-task and within-task complementarity -> allocation among automation, augmentation, and unaided human work -> substitution, augmentation, and human-resource reallocation contributions to average task performance
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Analytical judgment-task framework validated with experimental classification of 100 images and 10,000 ex post simulation runs under a fixed task set, human-resource budget, and average-performance objective
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Automation is favored where AI is relatively strong and tasks differ in human-versus-AI advantage; augmentation is most useful where humans can discriminate correct from incorrect advice and performances are similar; scarce humans are reallocated toward tasks difficult for AI
limitations: The model fixes task count, human resources, and an average-accuracy objective rather than wages, profit, welfare, liability, or task value
Image classification with observable ground truth does not represent every creative, strategic, relational, or unstructured task
The allocation requires expected performance and complementarity information that organizations may not possess
Human heterogeneity in ability and advice discrimination is not fully modeled
Repeated AI use may weaken tacit knowledge, changing complementarity and the appropriate allocation over time

anti_patterns: Do not describe augmentation as inherently preferable to automation or unaided human work.
Do not count released human capacity as a benefit unless it is productively reallocated.
Do not transfer image-classification optima mechanically to knowledge work.
Do not hold the human-AI capability frontier fixed in a longitudinal claim.

verified_admissions.title: Artificial Intelligence and Strategic Decision-Making: Evidence from Entrepreneurs and Investors

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access INFORMS article, pages 322-345, including prompt appendices

verified_extraction.claim_path: current LLM generation and evaluation of business plans -> comparison with accelerator applicants and experienced investor judgments -> potential changes in strategic search, representation, aggregation, and competitive dynamics
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Two entrepreneurship settings: 309 applications from a European accelerator, with blinded evaluator comparisons generating 2,500 plan ratings, and 138 competition business plans scored by both an LLM and experienced investors
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: LLM-generated plans scored better on average largely by improving the lower tail rather than accepted plans; LLM and investor scores were positively correlated but left most variation unexplained; the move from faster strategic search to profitability depends on execution, distinctiveness, and competition
limitations: Business-plan ratings and stated investment likelihood are not realized funding, execution, survival, revenue, or profit
A within-evaluator blinded comparison identifies document-level ratings rather than returns from organizational adoption
The evaluation study contains 138 plans and correlations do not establish interchangeable human and AI judgment
Current LLM outputs may cluster around well-represented strategies and can reproduce training-data biases
Many firm-performance and market-structure implications are scenarios rather than observed causal effects

anti_patterns: Do not equate a better-rated business plan with a better business.
Do not equate faster or broader strategic search with profit or durable advantage.
Do not call correlated AI and investor scores equivalent judgment.
Do not narrate capability scenarios as observed competitive outcomes.

verified_admissions.title: The Unequal Adoption of ChatGPT Exacerbates Existing Inequalities Among Workers
verified_admissions.journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access PNAS article and supplementary appendix through PubMed Central
sections_reviewed: Statistics Denmark sampling and register linkage
ever, recent, work, and core-task adoption measures

verified_extraction.claim_path: worker characteristics, beliefs, employer rules, and training needs -> ever, recent, work, and core-task ChatGPT use -> unequal access to potential task-level time savings and limited short-run task reallocation
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: About 18,000 valid complete responses from 100,000 invited Danish workers in eleven exposed occupations, fielded from November 2023 through January 2024 and linked to administrative employment, earnings, education, wealth, and demographic records
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Use differs sharply by occupation, age, experience, prior earnings, and gender; perceived time savings alone weakly predict use; an information treatment shifts beliefs but not actual two-week use, consistent with employer restrictions and training needs binding
limitations: The sample covers eleven exposed occupations in Denmark rather than all workers, firms, or countries
Most adoption, beliefs, time savings, frictions, and intended use measures are self-reported
Potential exposure is inherited from task ratings and is not observed production use or realized productivity
The short follow-up cannot measure organizational reconfiguration, durable skill effects, wages, output, or long-run inequality
Associations between worker characteristics and prior use are not causal treatment effects

anti_patterns: Do not equate awareness, ever use, work use, core-task use, and recent active use.
Do not infer realized productivity from believed time savings or task exposure.
Do not attribute the observed adoption gaps solely to worker preferences when firm restrictions and training bind.
Do not generalize a Danish exposed-occupation survey directly to economy-wide output or inequality.

verified_admissions.title: Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: A Field Experiment

whole_text_audit.access: Complete open-access INFORMS article, pages 57-72, including online appendices and data references
sections_reviewed: workflow, authority, training, and incentive interventions

verified_extraction.claim_path: the same AI sales system embedded in either tailored or untailored work procedures, authority, training, and incentives -> utilization and workflow response -> sales-meeting and units-sold performance measures
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Balanced panel of 1,584 quarterly person observations from sales experts in business units of one multinational pharmaceutical company, analyzed with individual and time fixed effects and business-unit clustered inference
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Interaction tailored to adaptor or innovator cognitive style improved the primary sales-meeting outcome relative to control, while untailored interaction reduced it; declining system use and role conflict help explain the adverse condition
limitations: Randomization occurred across a small number of business-unit clusters, producing low statistical power and constraining causal interpretation
The primary outcome is sales meetings; units sold are more delayed and the tailored-condition estimate is not statistically distinguishable on that measure
One pharmaceutical sales setting may not generalize to other functions, industries, countries, or collective outcomes
The intervention bundles work procedures, authority, training, and incentives, limiting isolation of any one component
Tailoring costs and possible within-group spillovers are not fully measured

anti_patterns: Do not attribute performance to the AI model independently of implementation context.
Do not call the treatment a universal cognitive-style prescription.
Do not equate more sales meetings with realized revenue or profit without the downstream measure.
Do not suppress the adverse untailored result or the study's small-cluster power constraint.

verified_atomic_observations.observation: Representative worker surveys require separate denominators for any use, work use, daily use, and assisted work hours.
Rapid extensive-margin adoption can coexist with shallow intensity when only a small share of total work hours is assisted.
Occupation, industry, age, education, and firm climate create material adoption heterogeneity.
Self-reported time savings are a transmission input, not verified firm productivity or aggregate output.
A production-use question yields a narrower adoption construct than testing, aspiration, invention, or AI-enabled product sales.
Firm-weighted adoption can be low while employment-weighted adoption is much higher because use concentrates in large employers.
Firm size, age, owner characteristics, sector, and geography shape diffusion and must survive any national average.
An adoption cross section maps diffusion but does not itself identify productivity, causality, or worker incidence.
Improving a prediction within one task can increase decision variation elsewhere in an interdependent organization.
Modularizing decisions can ease AI adoption while sacrificing synergies created by interdependence.
Coordination mechanisms can turn organizational interdependence from an adoption barrier into a source of value.
Task capability and system-wide productive use are different analytical states.
Randomized access on bounded professional writing tasks identifies a task treatment, not a complete job redesign.
Productivity assessment should carry both completion time and independently graded quality.
Larger gains among lower initial performers can compress within-task performance inequality.
A worker-task productivity effect cannot be promoted to firm revenue, employment, or aggregate TFP without added links.
A staggered production rollout provides stronger workflow evidence than a laboratory capability benchmark.
Worker effects vary sharply by prior skill and tenure, including possible quality declines among top performers.
Resolved issues per hour decomposes into handling time, concurrency, resolution, and quality rather than a single speed metric.
Medium-run gains in one firm do not determine wages, total labor demand, or longer-run equilibrium adjustment.
Actual voluntary use of predictive AI in a field setting links adoption to observed task productivity.
A prediction tool can substitute for a skill component and therefore benefit lower-skill workers more.
Search-time efficiency is a task outcome and should not be relabeled as daily income or total output.
Single-city and single-occupation evidence requires an explicit external-validity boundary.
Individual quality and collective output diversity are separate outcome dimensions that can move in opposite directions.
Baseline creativity conditions who benefits from AI-generated ideas.
An individually rational productivity aid can create a collective homogenization cost.
Deployment design and input uniformity are part of the treatment and limit generalization to configurable systems.
Randomized workplace trials across three firms improve external validity while retaining company-level heterogeneity.
Tool access, adoption, and completed tasks are sequentially distinct measurements.
Less-experienced developers can have both higher take-up and larger productivity gains.
Completed tasks omit maintainability, error costs, and business value unless those outcomes are measured separately.
AI-skilled employee resumes and postings measure firm investment, not direct deployed use.
AI investment is associated with sales, employment, valuation, and product innovation rather than only cost cutting.
AI-linked growth concentrating in initially large firms can increase industry concentration.
Firm growth may include business stealing, so firm estimates do not establish aggregate net growth.
Firm-survey adoption indicators and intensity measures provide distinct tests of the productivity relationship.
Cross-sectional, panel, and instrumental-variable estimates form an identification ladder rather than equivalent proof.
Country institutions, industrial mix, and survey definitions constrain external validity.
Firm productivity evidence does not reveal worker compensation, labor share, or aggregate spillovers by itself.
Occupational exposure can be constructed by mapping AI applications to the abilities used in occupations.
Occupation exposure can be aggregated to industries and geographies only through explicit employment weights.
Direction-neutral exposure cannot decide whether AI complements or substitutes for workers.
Exposure is neither adoption nor an observed employment, wage, productivity, or displacement outcome.
A task can be technically exposed under a time-and-quality rubric even when no worker or firm uses the tool.
Direct-model and software-augmented scenarios are modeled capability regimes, not observed adoption paths.
LLM exposure extends into higher-income knowledge work unlike many earlier automation measures.
Potential task impact must never be translated directly into jobs lost or a timetable for displacement.
Augmentation innovations create new work and raise occupational labor demand while automation innovations erode it.
The locus of new work changes across eras and skill groups, making historical averages regime-dependent.
Demand shocks and innovation direction jointly determine whether new tasks appear.
Automation and augmentation can rise together within occupations while exerting opposite labor-demand effects.
Local industry composition can transmit national technology adoption into heterogeneous commuting-zone employment effects.
Estimated employment incidence differs by sector, skill, production status, and wage rank.
A shift-share design requires explicit instrument and local-composition qualifications.
Negative local relative effects do not mechanically imply the same national aggregate employment effect.
Aggregate gains require both the share of tasks affected and the average cost saving on those tasks.
Easy-to-learn task evidence can overstate gains on context-dependent tasks with noisy objectives.
A calibrated ten-year TFP range is a scenario conditional on inputs, not an observed current outcome.
Adoption, complementary change, prices, demand, wages, and distribution mediate the path from task savings to macro outcomes.
AI assistance can improve and degrade performance on adjacent tasks within the same professional workflow.
Completion, speed, subjective quality, and objective correctness can move differently under the same tool treatment.
A realistic laboratory-in-the-field experiment remains distinct from sustained production integration and endogenous use.
A capability frontier is model-, task-, workflow-, and time-specific, so it must be recalibrated rather than frozen.
Worker-level productivity potential can coexist with short-run substitution in the market for exposed services.
Employment probability, conditional job count, total contracts, and platform earnings are separate labor-market margins.
High prior quality need not protect workers when the technology changes buyer demand for the service itself.
A short-run online-platform response cannot determine total employment, wages, welfare, or long-run equilibrium adjustment.
Organizational adaptation can begin through selective changes in demanded organizing skills before realized production effects are observable.
Information provision, task division, monitoring, and operational exception handling are analytically distinct organizing functions.
A job-posting response records intended labor demand rather than filled employment or completed organizational redesign.
Stronger post-GPT-4 responses show that organizational adaptation depends on capability regime as well as elapsed time.
Adoption intensity can matter nonlinearly even when the extensive margin simply records whether a firm uses AI.
Employee job satisfaction is a distinct outcome from output, speed, pay, autonomy, retention, and firm value.
Exploration orientation and data governance can change how adoption intensity translates into employee experience.
Earnings-call AI language and self-selected employee reviews require explicit proxy and selection qualifications.
AI adoption can increase demand for managers while reducing demand for selected routine managerial skills.
Managerial skill demand can shift toward coordination, adaptation, creativity, growth, and data use as AI investment deepens.
Managerial complementarity varies with industry and firm R&D intensity rather than applying uniformly.
AI-skill vacancy share, managerial postings, filled jobs, and deployed AI are non-equivalent measurements.
The relationship between AI exposure and employment varies across countries, worker skill, age composition, and institutional regimes.
Employment-share gains in exposed occupations need not be accompanied by relative-wage gains.
Occupation exposure can organize heterogeneous labor evidence but cannot identify actual firm adoption.
Country-level diffusion, education, competition, and employment-protection correlations remain suggestive rather than isolated causal mechanisms.
High fixed costs, low operating costs, and economies of scope can concentrate provider value even when model capabilities are widely useful.
Fierce foundation-model competition can coexist with concentrated upstream compute, cloud, data, or talent inputs.
Open-source distribution can expand consumer surplus and downstream innovation without generating equivalent provider revenue.
Market structure is regime-dependent because capability convergence, breakthroughs, prices, demand, vertical ties, and entry can move rapidly.
Any adoption and adoption intensity can yield different conclusions about firm performance.
Data systems, cloud infrastructure, and firm-specific R&D can condition whether adoption translates into revenue growth.
Testing and low-intensity use may precede detectable payoff while firms accumulate complements and redesign processes.
An observational revenue-growth threshold is evidence of conditional association, not a universal causal adoption threshold.
Organizational change, training, data, process redesign, and other intangibles are productive complements rather than free add-ons to a general-purpose technology.
Measured productivity can lag during complementary investment and rise later when accumulated intangible capital yields services.
A productivity J-curve is a conditional measurement mechanism, not proof that every technology investment will pay off.
Measured TFP, true productivity, output, revenue, profit, and welfare remain distinct outcomes across the investment cycle.
AI-vacancy posting is a narrow establishment-adoption proxy rather than direct observation of installed systems or workflow use.
An adopting establishment can reduce non-AI vacancy demand while changing the skill mix of the positions it continues to post.
A visible establishment response can remain too small to detect after aggregation to occupations or industries.
A statistically undetectable aggregate effect is not proof of a precisely zero economic effect.
An individual with AI can match selected average-quality benefits of a small human team in a bounded task without proving that AI replaces sustained teamwork.
AI can help workers cross functional expertise boundaries, changing the coordination value of organizational silos and teams.
Higher average idea quality can coexist with weaker identification of the best idea, so generation and selection are distinct outcome stages.
Rated early-stage solutions from a one-day single-firm experiment do not establish implementation, commercial value, jobs, or aggregate productivity.
The best work configuration depends on relative capability and whether complementarity occurs across tasks or within one advised task.
Automation creates an organizational gain through released labor only when that labor is reallocated productively.
Augmentation can erode tacit knowledge over time, altering future complementarity and substitution risk.
A task allocation that maximizes average accuracy under fixed resources does not by itself optimize cost, wages, profit, task value, or welfare.
An LLM can improve evaluated business-plan quality chiefly in the lower tail without improving plans already selected by an accelerator.
Positive correlation between AI and investor evaluations supports screening relevance but not interchangeable judgment.
Faster and cheaper strategic search can improve candidate options without guaranteeing execution, profit, or durable competitive advantage.
Claims about AI reshaping competition depend on capability and market scenarios and should remain separate from observed document-level evidence.
Awareness, ever use, work use, core-task use, and recent use are successive adoption measures with different denominators.
Adoption gaps within exposed occupations can persist by gender, age, experience, and prior earnings even after task and workplace controls.
Correcting beliefs about potential time savings may not change actual use when employer restrictions and training needs bind.
Task-level time savings need not expand output or reallocate work before organizations redesign workflows.
The same AI system can improve or reduce observed performance depending on how workflow, authority, training, and incentives structure its use.
System availability does not establish durable utilization when role conflict and implementation friction cause use to decline.
Worker-level fit can moderate AI implementation, but one bundled, underpowered field treatment does not establish a universal tailoring rule.
A positive primary process measure and a statistically uncertain downstream sales measure should remain separate in performance narration.
